en.title: Operators, == and hashCode
en.summary: Define operators on your Dart classes, compare objects by value with == and hashCode, and sort them with Comparable, using a Money type.
body: In Dart, operators are methods with a special name: **`operator +`**, `operator *`, `operator <`… `Money` stores cents and a currency, and defines `+` to add amounts (throwing an `ArgumentError` when the currencies differ), `*` to multiply by a quantity and `<` to compare. That way, `coffee * 2 + croissant` reads like a café bill.

By default, `==` compares identity: two objects are equal only if they are the same object. To make two `Money(150)` equal you override **`operator ==`**, which takes an `Object`, checks the type with `is Money` and compares the fields. `identical` still says `false`: they are equal, but not the same object.

Golden rule: if you override `==`, override **`hashCode`** too, so that equal objects produce the same number. `Object.hash(cents, currency)` computes it from the same fields `==` compares. Sets and maps rely on it to look things up, which is why the set `{coffee, Money(150), croissant}` ends up with only two prices.

Implementing **`Comparable<Money>`** with `compareTo` gives the class a natural order, and `sort()` uses it with no extra arguments. `toString()` decides how the object is printed, inside lists and sets too. The last case shows the error when adding euros to dollars.
points: `operator +` and friends define operators on your classes.
Override `==` to compare by value.
`==` always goes with `hashCode`, computed from the same fields.
`Object.hash` combines several fields into one hash code.
`Comparable` and `compareTo` let `sort()` order your objects.
en.exercise: Add `operator -` to `Money` and work out the change a customer gets when paying the order with a 5-euro note (`Money(500)`).

advanced.html: class Money implements Comparable<Money> {  final int cents;  final String currency;  const Money(this.cents, [this.currency = 'EUR']);  Money operator +(Money other) {    if (other.currency != currency) throw ArgumentError('$currency + ${other.currency}');    return Money(cents + other.cents, currency);  }  Money operator *(int times) => Money(cents * times, currency);  bool operator <(Money other) => cents < other.cents;  @override  int compareTo(Money other) => cents.compareTo(other.cents); // for sort()  // Equal by value: same amount and currency. hashCode must agree with ==.  @override  bool operator ==(Object other) =>      other is Money && other.cents == cents && other.currency == currency;  @override  int get hashCode => Object.hash(cents, currency);  @override  String toString() => '${(cents / 100).toStringAsFixed(2)} $currency';}void main() {  final coffee = Money(150), croissant = Money(195);  print('Order: ${coffee * 2 + croissant}, cheaper: ${coffee < croissant}');  print('== ${Money(150) == coffee}, identical ${identical(Money(150), coffee)}');  print('Distinct prices: ${{coffee, Money(150), croissant}}'); // a Set  print('Sorted: ${[Money(999), coffee, croissant]..sort()}');  try { coffee + Money(150, 'USD'); } on ArgumentError catch (e) { print('Cannot add ${e.message}'); }}
advanced.output:
Order: 4.95 EUR, cheaper: true
== true, identical false
Distinct prices: {1.50 EUR, 1.95 EUR}
Sorted: [1.50 EUR, 1.95 EUR, 9.99 EUR]
Cannot add EUR + USD

es.title: Futures, async y await
es.summary: Entienda las Future de Dart y escriba código asíncrono legible con async y await, simulando llamadas a un servidor con Future.delayed.
body: Una **`Future<T>`** es la promesa de un valor de tipo `T` que llegará más tarde: la respuesta de un servidor, un archivo leído o el resultado de una consulta. `fetchUser` y `fetchOrders` simulan una llamada de red con `Future.delayed`, que espera unos milisegundos sin bloquear el programa.

Una función marcada como **`async`** siempre devuelve una `Future`, aunque dentro haga `return` de un valor normal: `countOrders` devuelve `Future<int>`. Dentro de ella se puede usar **`await`**, que pausa esa función hasta que la `Future` termina y entrega su valor.

Fíjese en el orden de la salida. `fetchUser(7)` arranca la petición y devuelve enseguida una `Future` pendiente, así que el mensaje 2 se escribe antes de tener el usuario. Solo `await pending` espera, y entonces aparece el 3. Después, `await fetchOrders(...)` espera la segunda llamada: con `await`, el código asíncrono se lee de arriba abajo, como el síncrono, y cada ejecución da la misma salida porque cada paso espera al anterior.

`then()` es el estilo anterior: registra una función que se ejecuta cuando llega el resultado. Sigue siendo útil, pero `async`/`await` es más legible. `main` también puede ser `async` y devolver `Future<void>`. En una aplicación Flutter, los datos de una pantalla se cargan exactamente así, con funciones `async` que devuelven el modelo ya listo.
points: Una `Future<T>` es un valor que llegará más tarde.
Una función `async` siempre devuelve una `Future`.
`await` pausa la función hasta tener el valor, sin bloquear el programa.
Llamar sin `await` arranca la tarea y el código sigue adelante.
`then()` es la alternativa con funciones de *callback*.
es.exercise: Escriba `fetchAddress(int userId)`, que tarde 30 ms y devuelva `'Calle Mayor 5, Madrid'`, y muestre la dirección entre el saludo y la lista de pedidos.

en.title: Futures, async and await
en.summary: Understand Dart Futures and write readable asynchronous code with async and await, simulating server calls with Future.delayed.
body: A **`Future<T>`** is the promise of a value of type `T` that will arrive later: a server response, a file that has been read or the result of a query. `fetchUser` and `fetchOrders` simulate a network call with `Future.delayed`, which waits a few milliseconds without blocking the program.

A function marked **`async`** always returns a `Future`, even when it `return`s a plain value: `countOrders` returns a `Future<int>`. Inside it you can use **`await`**, which pauses that function until the `Future` completes and hands over its value.

Look at the order of the output. `fetchUser(7)` starts the request and immediately returns a pending `Future`, so message 2 is printed before the user is there. Only `await pending` waits, and then line 3 appears. Next, `await fetchOrders(...)` waits for the second call: with `await`, asynchronous code reads from top to bottom like synchronous code, and every run gives the same output because each step waits for the previous one.

`then()` is the older style: it registers a function that runs when the result arrives. It is still useful, but `async`/`await` is easier to read. `main` itself can be `async` and return `Future<void>`. In a Flutter app, a screen's data is loaded exactly like this, with `async` functions that return the ready-made model.
points: A `Future<T>` is a value that will arrive later.
An `async` function always returns a `Future`.
`await` pauses the function until the value is ready, without blocking the program.
Calling without `await` starts the work and carries on.
`then()` is the callback-based alternative.
en.exercise: Write `fetchAddress(int userId)`, which takes 30 ms and returns `'Calle Mayor 5, Madrid'`, and print the address between the greeting and the order list.

advanced.html: // Pretend network calls: a Future is a value that arrives later.Future<Map<String, Object>> fetchUser(int id) async {  await Future.delayed(const Duration(milliseconds: 80));  return {'id': id, 'name': 'Elena', 'plan': 'pro'};}Future<List<String>> fetchOrders(int userId) async {  await Future.delayed(const Duration(milliseconds: 40));  return ['#1001 headphones', '#1002 phone case'];}// An async function always returns a Future, even with a plain return.Future<int> countOrders(int userId) async => (await fetchOrders(userId)).length;Future<void> main() async {  print('1. Asking for user 7');  final pending = fetchUser(7); // starts now, does not block  print('2. Main keeps going while the request is in flight');  final user = await pending; // pause here until the value arrives  print('3. Hello, ${user['name']} (${user['plan']} plan)');  // await runs one call after the other, like normal code.  final orders = await fetchOrders(user['id'] as int);  for (final order in orders) {    print('   $order');  }  // The older style: register a callback with then().  await countOrders(7).then((n) => print('4. $n orders in total'));  print('5. Done');}
advanced.output:
1. Asking for user 7
2. Main keeps going while the request is in flight
3. Hello, Elena (pro plan)
   #1001 headphones
   #1002 phone case
4. 2 orders in total
5. Done

es.title: Future.wait y errores asíncronos
es.summary: Lance varias peticiones en paralelo con Future.wait en Dart y trate sus errores con try/catch, timeout y onError, con una salida siempre igual.
body: Con `await` una tras otra, tres llamadas de 60, 10 y 30 ms tardarían 100 ms. **`Future.wait`** las lanza todas a la vez y espera a que acaben, así que tarda lo que la más lenta. Lo importante para un resultado predecible es que la lista de resultados sigue el **orden de la lista de entrada**, no el orden en que terminan: por eso `Stocks` sale siempre `[35, 63, 21]`.

`fetchStock` lanza `StateError` con los códigos que empiezan por `X`. Dentro de una función `async`, una excepción hace que su `Future` termine con error, y al hacer `await` ese error se lanza de nuevo en quien espera. Por eso basta un `try`/`catch` normal, con `on StateError`, alrededor de `await Future.wait(...)`.

Para esperar a la vez futures de **tipos distintos**, Dart 3 permite agruparlas en un record y usar `.wait`: `(Future.value('Mug'), fetchStock(...)).wait` devuelve un record `(String, int)` que se desestructura en `name` y `stock`, cada uno con su tipo.

**`timeout`** convierte una llamada demasiado lenta en una `TimeoutException`, que viene de `dart:async`: `SLOW-API` tarda 300 ms y se abandona a los 50. Y cuando un fallo no es grave, **`onError`** sustituye el error por un valor de reserva: el producto desconocido da `0` en vez de una excepción.
points: `Future.wait` ejecuta en paralelo y devuelve los resultados en orden.
Un error en una `Future` reaparece en el `await`: captúrelo con `try`/`catch`.
`(f1, f2).wait` espera futures de tipos distintos.
`timeout` pone un límite de tiempo a una llamada.
`onError` devuelve un valor de reserva si algo falla.
es.exercise: Añada un tercer elemento al record, `fetchStock('CAP', 15)`, desestructúrelo en una variable `caps` y escriba los tres valores en una línea.

en.title: Future.wait and async errors
en.summary: Run several requests in parallel with Future.wait in Dart and handle their errors with try/catch, timeout and onError, with output that never changes.
body: Awaited one after another, three calls of 60, 10 and 30 ms would take 100 ms. **`Future.wait`** starts them all at once and waits for them to finish, so it takes as long as the slowest. The key to a predictable result is that the list of results follows the **order of the input list**, not the order in which they finish: that is why `Stocks` always prints `[35, 63, 21]`.

`fetchStock` throws a `StateError` for codes starting with `X`. Inside an `async` function, an exception makes its `Future` complete with an error, and `await` rethrows that error in whoever is waiting. So an ordinary `try`/`catch` with `on StateError` around `await Future.wait(...)` is all it takes.

To wait for futures of **different types** at the same time, Dart 3 lets you group them in a record and call `.wait`: `(Future.value('Mug'), fetchStock(...)).wait` returns a `(String, int)` record that is destructured into `name` and `stock`, each with its own type.

**`timeout`** turns a call that is too slow into a `TimeoutException`, which comes from `dart:async`: `SLOW-API` takes 300 ms and is abandoned after 50. And when a failure is not serious, **`onError`** replaces the error with a fallback value: the unknown product gives `0` instead of an exception.
points: `Future.wait` runs in parallel and returns the results in order.
An error in a `Future` resurfaces at the `await`: catch it with `try`/`catch`.
`(f1, f2).wait` waits for futures of different types.
`timeout` puts a time limit on a call.
`onError` returns a fallback value when something fails.
en.exercise: Add a third element to the record, `fetchStock('CAP', 15)`, destructure it into a `caps` variable and print all three values on one line.

advanced.html: import 'dart:async';Future<int> fetchStock(String sku, int ms) async {  await Future.delayed(Duration(milliseconds: ms)); // simulated network  if (sku.startsWith('X')) throw StateError('unknown product $sku');  return sku.length * 7;}Future<void> main() async {  // In parallel: results come back in list order, not in finishing order.  final stocks = await Future.wait(      [fetchStock('MUG-1', 60), fetchStock('TSHIRT-22', 10), fetchStock('CAP', 30)]);  print('Stocks: $stocks');  // If one fails, await throws and an ordinary try/catch handles it.  try {    await Future.wait([fetchStock('MUG-1', 10), fetchStock('X-404', 5)]);  } on StateError catch (e) {    print('Failed: ${e.message}');  }  // A record of futures of different types, awaited together.  final (name, stock) = await (Future.value('Mug'), fetchStock('MUG-1', 20)).wait;  print('$name: $stock in stock');  // A timeout turns a call that is too slow into an error.  try {    await fetchStock('SLOW-API', 300).timeout(const Duration(milliseconds: 50));  } on TimeoutException {    print('Gave up after 50 ms');  }  // Or recover with a fallback value instead of an exception.  print('Fallback: ${await fetchStock('X-1', 5).onError((e, _) => 0)}');}
advanced.output:
Stocks: [35, 63, 21]
Failed: unknown product X-404
Mug: 35 in stock
Gave up after 50 ms
Fallback: 0

es.title: Streams con async* y await for
es.summary: Cree streams en Dart con funciones async* y yield, recórralos con await for y transfórmelos con where y map, con una descarga simulada.
body: Una `Future` da un solo valor; un **`Stream`** da una secuencia de valores a lo largo del tiempo: el progreso de una descarga, los mensajes de un chat o las lecturas de un sensor. La forma más sencilla de crear uno es una función **`async*`**: cada **`yield`** emite un evento, y entre uno y otro la función puede hacer `await`.

`download` simula la descarga de 600 KB en trozos de 160: espera 20 ms por trozo, suma lo recibido sin pasarse del total y emite el porcentaje. Además, nada se ejecuta hasta que alguien escucha el stream.

**`await for`** recorre el stream: espera cada evento, ejecuta el cuerpo del bucle y continúa hasta que el stream se cierra, que aquí es cuando la función termina. Después de las cuatro líneas de progreso, `main` sigue con lo siguiente.

Los streams tienen los mismos métodos que las listas (`where`, `map`, `fold`, `toList`…), pero asíncronos: `toList()` devuelve una `Future`. `Stream.fromIterable` convierte una lista en stream, y del ejemplo se quedan las lecturas de más de 24 grados. `Stream.periodic` emite un número cada 10 ms y no termina nunca; un **`break`** dentro de `await for` cancela la suscripción y el stream se detiene.
points: Un `Stream` es una secuencia de valores asíncronos.
Una función `async*` crea un stream, y `yield` emite cada valor.
`await for` espera cada evento hasta que el stream se cierra.
`where`, `map` y `toList` también existen para streams.
`break` dentro de `await for` cancela la suscripción.
es.exercise: Cree `Stream<String> countdown(int from) async*` que emita `3`, `2`, `1` y `Go!` con 50 ms entre cada valor, y recórralo con `await for`.

en.title: Streams with async* and await for
en.summary: Create Dart streams with async* functions and yield, consume them with await for and transform them with where and map, using a simulated download.
body: A `Future` delivers one value; a **`Stream`** delivers a sequence of values over time: a download's progress, chat messages or sensor readings. The simplest way to create one is an **`async*`** function: each **`yield`** emits an event, and in between the function may `await`.

`download` simulates downloading 600 KB in 160 KB chunks: it waits 20 ms per chunk, adds up what has arrived without going past the total and emits the percentage. Also, nothing runs until someone listens to the stream.

**`await for`** walks through the stream: it waits for each event, runs the loop body and carries on until the stream closes, which here happens when the function ends. After the four progress lines, `main` moves on.

Streams have the same methods as lists (`where`, `map`, `fold`, `toList`…), only asynchronous: `toList()` returns a `Future`. `Stream.fromIterable` turns a list into a stream, and the example keeps the readings above 24 degrees. `Stream.periodic` emits a number every 10 ms and never ends; a **`break`** inside `await for` cancels the subscription and the stream stops.
points: A `Stream` is a sequence of asynchronous values.
An `async*` function creates a stream, and `yield` emits each value.
`await for` waits for each event until the stream closes.
`where`, `map` and `toList` exist for streams too.
`break` inside `await for` cancels the subscription.
en.exercise: Create `Stream<String> countdown(int from) async*` that emits `3`, `2`, `1` and `Go!` with 50 ms between values, and loop over it with `await for`.

advanced.html: // async* returns a Stream: each yield sends one event, over time.Stream<int> download(int totalKb, int chunkKb) async* {  var received = 0;  while (received < totalKb) {    await Future.delayed(const Duration(milliseconds: 20)); // a network chunk    received += chunkKb;    if (received > totalKb) received = totalKb;    yield received * 100 ~/ totalKb;  }}Future<void> main() async {  // await for waits for each event until the stream closes.  await for (final percent in download(600, 160)) {    print('Downloaded $percent%');  }  // Streams have where, map, fold... like lists, but asynchronous.  final readings = Stream.fromIterable([18.5, 21.0, 25.4, 30.1, 27.9]);  final hot = await readings.where((t) => t > 24).map((t) => '$t C').toList();  print('Hot readings: $hot');  // A stream that never ends: break cancels the subscription.  final ticks = Stream.periodic(const Duration(milliseconds: 10), (i) => i + 1);  await for (final tick in ticks) {    if (tick > 3) break;    print('Tick $tick');  }  print('Stopped listening');}

Downloaded 26%
Downloaded 53%
Downloaded 80%
Downloaded 100%
Hot readings: [25.4 C, 30.1 C, 27.9 C]
Tick 1
Tick 2
Tick 3
Stopped listening

es.title: StreamController y eventos
es.summary: Emita sus propios eventos en Dart con StreamController y escúchelos con listen, onError y onDone, con un carrito de la compra de ejemplo.
body: Cuando los eventos no salen de un bucle sino de acciones sueltas (un toque en un botón, un mensaje que llega), se usa un **`StreamController`**. Tiene dos caras: una para meter eventos (`add`, `addError`, `close`) y otra, `stream`, para escucharlos. `Cart` guarda el controlador en un campo privado y solo expone `events`, de modo que desde fuera se puede escuchar pero no emitir.

`add` actualiza las cantidades y emite un texto con el total de artículos; `remove` emite un evento normal si el artículo estaba y, si no, un **error** con `addError`. Un controlador normal admite un único oyente; creado con **`.broadcast()`**, admite cualquier número, como aquí.

**`listen`** suscribe una función que recibe cada evento y admite dos más: `onError` para los errores y `onDone` para cuando el stream se cierra. El segundo oyente, la insignia del carrito, filtra con `where` y solo atiende a los añadidos. También lleva `onError`, aunque esté vacío: en un stream broadcast, un error que llega a un oyente sin `onError` se considera no capturado y detiene el programa.

Los eventos se entregan de forma asíncrona, pero en el orden en que se emitieron y a los oyentes en el orden en que se suscribieron, así que la salida es la misma en cada ejecución. `close()` envía la señal de fin a todos y devuelve una `Future` que `main` espera; por eso `cart closed` es lo último. Este patrón, una clase que expone un stream de cambios, es la base de arquitecturas como BLoC, muy usadas en Flutter.
points: `StreamController` permite emitir eventos cuando usted quiera.
`add` emite un valor, `addError` un error y `close` cierra el stream.
`.broadcast()` admite varios oyentes a la vez.
`listen` recibe cada evento, y además `onError` y `onDone`.
Exponga solo `stream` y guarde el controlador como privado.
es.exercise: Añada un método `clear()` que vacíe el carrito y emita `cleared`, y un tercer oyente que cuente los eventos recibidos y escriba el total en `onDone`.

en.title: StreamController and events
en.summary: Emit your own events in Dart with a StreamController and listen to them with listen, onError and onDone, using a shopping cart as the example.
body: When events do not come from a loop but from one-off actions (a button tap, an incoming message), you use a **`StreamController`**. It has two sides: one to put events in (`add`, `addError`, `close`) and another, `stream`, to listen to them. `Cart` keeps the controller in a private field and only exposes `events`, so outside code can listen but not emit.

`add` updates the quantities and emits a message with the total number of items; `remove` emits a normal event if the item was there and, if not, an **error** through `addError`. A regular controller allows a single listener; created with **`.broadcast()`**, it allows any number, as here.

**`listen`** subscribes a function that receives each event and accepts two more: `onError` for errors and `onDone` for when the stream closes. The second listener, the cart badge, filters with `where` and only cares about additions. It still has an `onError`, even an empty one: on a broadcast stream, an error reaching a listener without `onError` counts as uncaught and stops the program.

Events are delivered asynchronously, but in the order they were emitted and to listeners in the order they subscribed, so the output is the same on every run. `close()` sends the done signal to everyone and returns a `Future` that `main` awaits, which is why `cart closed` comes last. This pattern, a class exposing a stream of changes, is the basis of architectures such as BLoC, widely used in Flutter.
points: A `StreamController` lets you emit events whenever you like.
`add` emits a value, `addError` an error and `close` closes the stream.
`.broadcast()` allows several listeners at once.
`listen` takes each event, plus `onError` and `onDone`.
Expose only the `stream` and keep the controller private.
en.exercise: Add a `clear()` method that empties the cart and emits `cleared`, plus a third listener that counts the events it receives and prints the count in `onDone`.

advanced.html: import 'dart:async';class Cart {  final Map<String, int> _items = {};  // broadcast: any number of listeners can subscribe.  final _events = StreamController<String>.broadcast();  Stream<String> get events => _events.stream;  void add(String item) {    _items.update(item, (qty) => qty + 1, ifAbsent: () => 1);    _events.add('added $item, total ${_items.values.fold(0, (a, b) => a + b)}');  }  void remove(String item) => _items.remove(item) == null      ? _events.addError(StateError('$item is not in the cart'))      : _events.add('removed $item');  Future<void> close() => _events.close(); // sends "done" to every listener}Future<void> main() async {  final cart = Cart();  cart.events.listen((e) => print('log:   $e'),      onError: (Object e) => print('log:   ERROR ${(e as StateError).message}'),      onDone: () => print('log:   cart closed'));  cart.events.where((e) => e.startsWith('added')).listen((e) => print('badge: $e'),      onError: (_) {});  cart..add('Coffee beans')..add('Milk')..remove('Sugar')..remove('Milk')      ..add('Coffee beans');  await cart.close();}
advanced.output:
log:   added Coffee beans, total 1
badge: added Coffee beans, total 1
log:   added Milk, total 2
badge: added Milk, total 2
log:   ERROR Sugar is not in the cart
log:   removed Milk
log:   added Coffee beans, total 2
badge: added Coffee beans, total 2
log:   cart closed

es.title: Isolates con Isolate.run
es.summary: Saque el cálculo pesado del hilo principal en Dart con Isolate.run, ejecute varios isolates en paralelo y capture sus errores.
body: Todo código de Dart se ejecuta dentro de un **isolate**: una unidad de ejecución con su propia memoria y su propio bucle de eventos. `async`/`await` sirve para esperar sin bloquear, pero no reparte el cálculo: si una función pasa un segundo calculando, el isolate principal se queda ocupado ese segundo y, en una aplicación Flutter, la interfaz se congela.

`countPrimes` es trabajo de CPU puro: una criba de Eratóstenes que marca los números compuestos en una lista de booleanos y cuenta los que quedan. **`Isolate.run`**, de `dart:isolate`, crea un isolate nuevo, ejecuta en él la función que recibe, devuelve el resultado como una `Future` y cierra el isolate. Mientras tanto, el isolate principal queda libre.

Varios `Isolate.run` a la vez aprovechan varios núcleos. Pueden terminar en cualquier orden, pero `Future.wait` devuelve los resultados en el orden de la lista y el programa los escribe al final, por eso la salida es siempre la misma. Los isolates **no comparten memoria**: lo que se envía y lo que vuelve se copia, así que no hay condiciones de carrera de las que preocuparse.

Si la función falla dentro del isolate, el error vuelve a quien llamó: `countPrimes(-1)` intenta crear una lista de tamaño negativo, lanza `RangeError` y el `try`/`catch` de `main` lo captura. En Flutter, la función `compute()` hace exactamente esto, y es la forma de procesar un JSON enorme o una imagen sin que la pantalla se detenga.
points: Cada isolate tiene su propia memoria: no comparten variables.
`async` no reparte el cálculo; otro isolate sí.
`Isolate.run` ejecuta una función en otro isolate y devuelve una `Future`.
Con `Future.wait`, los resultados siguen el orden de la lista.
Los errores del isolate se capturan con `try`/`catch` en quien espera.
es.exercise: Escriba una función `sumOfSquares(int n)` que sume los cuadrados de 1 a `n`, y ejecute en paralelo `n = 1000` y `n = 1000000` con `Isolate.run`.

en.title: Isolates with Isolate.run
en.summary: Move heavy computation off Dart's main thread with Isolate.run, run several isolates in parallel and catch their errors.
body: All Dart code runs inside an **isolate**: a unit of execution with its own memory and its own event loop. `async`/`await` lets you wait without blocking, but it does not spread the computation: if a function spends a second crunching numbers, the main isolate is busy for that second and, in a Flutter app, the UI freezes.

`countPrimes` is pure CPU work: a sieve of Eratosthenes that marks composite numbers in a list of booleans and counts the rest. **`Isolate.run`**, from `dart:isolate`, spawns a new isolate, runs the given function there, returns the result as a `Future` and shuts the isolate down. Meanwhile, the main isolate stays free.

Several `Isolate.run` calls at once make use of several cores. They may finish in any order, but `Future.wait` returns the results in list order and the program prints them at the end, so the output is always the same. Isolates **share no memory**: whatever is sent and returned is copied, so there are no race conditions to worry about.

If the function fails inside the isolate, the error travels back to the caller: `countPrimes(-1)` tries to create a list of negative length, throws a `RangeError`, and the `try`/`catch` in `main` catches it. In Flutter, the `compute()` function does exactly this, and it is how you process a huge JSON file or an image without the screen stalling.
points: Each isolate has its own memory: no shared variables.
`async` does not spread computation; another isolate does.
`Isolate.run` runs a function in another isolate and returns a `Future`.
With `Future.wait`, results follow the order of the list.
Errors from the isolate are caught with `try`/`catch` by the caller.
en.exercise: Write a `sumOfSquares(int n)` function that adds the squares from 1 to `n`, and run `n = 1000` and `n = 1000000` in parallel with `Isolate.run`.

advanced.html: import 'dart:isolate';// CPU-heavy work: count the primes below [limit] with a sieve.int countPrimes(int limit) {  final composite = List<bool>.filled(limit, false);  var count = 0;  for (var n = 2; n < limit; n++) {    if (composite[n]) continue;    count++;    for (var m = n * n; m < limit; m += n) composite[m] = true;  }  return count;}Future<void> main() async {  // Isolate.run runs the function in another isolate (another core)  // and returns its result as a Future: main stays free meanwhile.  final primes = await Isolate.run(() => countPrimes(5000000));  print('Primes below 5,000,000: $primes');  // Several isolates at once; Future.wait keeps the order of the list.  final limits = [1000, 100000, 1000000];  final counts = await Future.wait([for (final n in limits) Isolate.run(() => countPrimes(n))]);  for (var i = 0; i < limits.length; i++) {    print('Below ${limits[i]}: ${counts[i]}');  }  // An exception inside the isolate comes back to the caller.  try {    await Isolate.run(() => countPrimes(-1));  } on RangeError {    print('The worker failed with a RangeError');  }}

es.title: JSON con fromJson y toJson
es.summary: Lea y escriba JSON en Dart con jsonDecode y jsonEncode, y conviértalo en objetos con tipos mediante fromJson y toJson, como en Flutter.
body: **`dart:convert`** trae lo necesario para trabajar con JSON. **`jsonDecode`** convierte el texto en estructuras de Dart: los objetos JSON pasan a `Map<String, dynamic>`, las listas a `List`, y los números, textos, booleanos y `null` a sus tipos. `body` es lo que podría responder una API: una lista con dos clientes (dos cadenas seguidas en el código se unen en una sola).

Trabajar con mapas por toda la aplicación es frágil, así que se convierten en objetos con tipo. El factory **`Customer.fromJson`** lee cada clave y la convierte a su tipo con `as`: `as String?` acepta el `null` de Pablo, y `List<String>.from(json['tags'] ?? const [])` convierte la lista dinámica en una lista de textos, o usa una vacía si la clave falta. Si el JSON trae un tipo inesperado, falla aquí, en un solo sitio, y no en mitad de la interfaz.

**`toJson`** hace el camino inverso: devuelve un mapa con tipos básicos. No hace falta llamarlo: **`jsonEncode`** llama por su cuenta a `toJson()` de cualquier objeto que no sepa convertir, y por eso `jsonEncode(customers.first)` funciona directamente.

Si el texto no es JSON válido (aquí, una coma sobrante), `jsonDecode` lanza `FormatException`. Esta pareja `fromJson`/`toJson` es la convención que siguen los modelos de cualquier aplicación Flutter; paquetes como `json_serializable` solo escriben este mismo código por usted.
points: `jsonDecode` convierte texto JSON en mapas y listas de Dart.
`fromJson` convierte el mapa en un objeto con tipos.
`toJson` devuelve un mapa, y `jsonEncode` lo usa automáticamente.
Use `as Tipo?` para los campos que pueden ser `null`.
Un JSON mal formado lanza `FormatException`.
es.exercise: Añada a `Customer` un campo `bool active` que en el JSON se llame `is_active` y valga `true` si falta, e inclúyalo en cada línea de la salida y en `toJson`.

en.title: JSON with fromJson and toJson
en.summary: Read and write JSON in Dart with jsonDecode and jsonEncode, and turn it into typed objects with fromJson and toJson, just as Flutter apps do.
body: **`dart:convert`** has everything needed to work with JSON. **`jsonDecode`** turns the text into Dart structures: JSON objects become `Map<String, dynamic>`, arrays become `List`, and numbers, strings, booleans and `null` map to their own types. `body` is what an API might send back: a list of two customers (two adjacent string literals in the code are joined into one).

Passing maps around the whole app is fragile, so they are turned into typed objects. The **`Customer.fromJson`** factory reads each key and casts it to its type with `as`: `as String?` accepts Pablo's `null`, and `List<String>.from(json['tags'] ?? const [])` turns the dynamic list into a list of strings, or uses an empty one when the key is missing. If the JSON carries an unexpected type, it fails here, in one place, not halfway through the UI.

**`toJson`** goes the other way: it returns a map of basic types. You do not even have to call it: **`jsonEncode`** calls `toJson()` by itself on any object it does not know how to convert, which is why `jsonEncode(customers.first)` just works.

If the text is not valid JSON (here, a trailing comma), `jsonDecode` throws a `FormatException`. This `fromJson`/`toJson` pair is the convention every Flutter app's models follow; packages such as `json_serializable` simply write this same code for you.
points: `jsonDecode` turns JSON text into Dart maps and lists.
`fromJson` turns the map into a typed object.
`toJson` returns a map, and `jsonEncode` uses it automatically.
Use `as Type?` for fields that may be `null`.
Malformed JSON throws a `FormatException`.
en.exercise: Add a `bool active` field to `Customer`, called `is_active` in the JSON and defaulting to `true` when missing, and include it in each output line and in `toJson`.

advanced.html: import 'dart:convert';class Customer {  final int id;  final String name;  final String? email;  final List<String> tags;  Customer({required this.id, required this.name, this.email, this.tags = const []});  // JSON arrives as Map<String, dynamic>: read each key with its type.  factory Customer.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> json) => Customer(        id: json['id'] as int,        name: json['name'] as String,        email: json['email'] as String?,        tags: List<String>.from(json['tags'] ?? const []),      );  Map<String, dynamic> toJson() => {'id': id, 'name': name, 'email': email, 'tags': tags};}const body = '[{"id": 17, "name": "Carmen Ruiz", "email": "carmen@example.com",'    ' "tags": ["vip"]}, {"id": 18, "name": "Pablo Gil", "email": null}]';void main() {  final list = jsonDecode(body) as List; // text -> Dart lists and maps  final customers = [for (final item in list) Customer.fromJson(item)];  for (final c in customers) {    print('#${c.id} ${c.name} <${c.email ?? 'no email'}> ${c.tags}');  }  print(jsonEncode(customers.first)); // jsonEncode calls toJson() for you  try { jsonDecode('{"id": 19,}'); } on FormatException catch (e) { print('Bad JSON: ${e.message}'); }}

#17 Carmen Ruiz <carmen@example.com> [vip]
#18 Pablo Gil <no email> []
{"id":17,"name":"Carmen Ruiz","email":"carmen@example.com","tags":["vip"]}
Bad JSON: Unexpected character

es.title: Iterables y generadores
es.summary: Genere secuencias perezosas en Dart con sync*, yield y yield*: trabaje con series infinitas y calcule solo lo que de verdad se pide.
body: Una función **`sync*`** devuelve un `Iterable` **perezoso**: su cuerpo no se ejecuta al llamarla, sino a medida que alguien pide valores, y cada **`yield`** entrega uno y deja la función en pausa hasta el siguiente. `invoiceNumbers` es un bucle sin fin, y no pasa nada: `skip(41).take(3)` pide justo los números 42 a 44 y la función no avanza más.

`readPrices` escribe una línea cada vez que entrega un precio, para ver cuándo trabaja. La cadena `readPrices().where(...).map(...)` todavía no lee nada: solo describe la consulta, y por eso `Query built, nothing read yet` sale antes que cualquier `reading`. Los métodos de `Iterable` como `where`, `map`, `skip` o `take` también son perezosos.

Al pedir `expensive.first` empieza el trabajo: se leen 120, 45 y 990, y al llegar al primero que supera 500 se le suma el IVA con aritmética entera (`* 121 ~/ 100`) y todo se detiene. Los precios 300 y 1500 no se leen nunca, algo que importa con miles de registros o con un origen de datos costoso. Ojo: si recorre `expensive` dos veces, la función se ejecuta dos veces; guarde el resultado con `toList()` si lo va a reutilizar.

**`yield*`** entrega todos los valores de otro iterable. `chunks` lo usa para ser recursiva: entrega el primer bloque de `size` elementos y delega el resto en otra llamada a sí misma. Es una forma cómoda de paginar una lista.
points: `sync*` devuelve un `Iterable` que se calcula al recorrerlo.
`yield` entrega un valor; `yield*`, todos los de otro iterable.
Un generador puede ser infinito si solo se piden unos cuantos valores.
`where`, `map`, `skip` y `take` no hacen nada hasta que se recorre el resultado.
Cada recorrido vuelve a ejecutar el generador; use `toList()` para guardarlo.
es.exercise: Escriba un generador infinito `fibonacci()` con `sync*` y muestre el primer número de Fibonacci mayor que 1000 con `firstWhere`.

en.title: Iterables and generators
en.summary: Produce lazy sequences in Dart with sync*, yield and yield*: work with infinite series and compute only what is actually requested.
body: A **`sync*`** function returns a **lazy** `Iterable`: its body does not run when you call it but as values are requested, and each **`yield`** hands over one value and pauses the function until the next request. `invoiceNumbers` is an endless loop, and that is fine: `skip(41).take(3)` asks for exactly numbers 42 to 44 and the function goes no further.

`readPrices` prints a line every time it hands over a price, so you can see when it works. The chain `readPrices().where(...).map(...)` reads nothing yet: it only describes the query, which is why `Query built, nothing read yet` appears before any `reading`. `Iterable` methods such as `where`, `map`, `skip` and `take` are lazy too.

Asking for `expensive.first` starts the work: 120, 45 and 990 are read, and on reaching the first one above 500 the VAT is added with integer arithmetic (`* 121 ~/ 100`) and everything stops. The prices 300 and 1500 are never read, which matters with thousands of records or an expensive data source. Beware: iterating over `expensive` twice runs the function twice; store the result with `toList()` if you are going to reuse it.

**`yield*`** hands over every value of another iterable. `chunks` uses it to be recursive: it yields the first block of `size` items and delegates the rest to another call to itself. It is a handy way to paginate a list.
points: `sync*` returns an `Iterable` that is computed as you iterate.
`yield` hands over one value; `yield*`, all the values of another iterable.
A generator can be infinite as long as you only ask for a few values.
`where`, `map`, `skip` and `take` do nothing until the result is iterated.
Each iteration reruns the generator; use `toList()` to keep the result.
en.exercise: Write an infinite `fibonacci()` generator with `sync*` and print the first Fibonacci number greater than 1000 using `firstWhere`.

advanced.html: // sync* returns a lazy Iterable: the body runs only as values are requested.Iterable<String> invoiceNumbers(String prefix) sync* {  for (var n = 1;; n++) {    yield '$prefix-${n.toString().padLeft(4, '0')}'; // infinite, and that's fine  }}Iterable<int> readPrices() sync* {  for (final price in [120, 45, 990, 300, 1500]) {    print('  reading $price');    yield price;  }}// yield* hands over every value of another iterable.Iterable<List<T>> chunks<T>(List<T> items, int size) sync* {  if (items.length <= size) {    yield items;    return;  }  yield items.sublist(0, size);  yield* chunks(items.sublist(size), size);}void main() {  print(invoiceNumbers('INV').skip(41).take(3).toList());  final expensive = readPrices().where((p) => p > 500).map((p) => p * 121 ~/ 100);  print('Query built, nothing read yet');  print('First expensive with VAT: ${expensive.first}'); // stops at 990  print('Pages: ${chunks(['ana', 'luis', 'eva', 'tom', 'iker'], 2).toList()}');}

es.title: Proyecto: procesar pedidos
es.summary: Combine clases selladas, genéricos, async y JSON en Dart en un pequeño sistema de pedidos: la lógica que hay detrás de una app Flutter.
body: Este programa reúne el curso en una pequeña capa de lógica de pedidos, la que tendría una aplicación Flutter debajo de sus pantallas. Empieza con un tipo **`Result<T>`** sellado y genérico: una operación termina en `Ok`, con un valor, o en `Err`, con un motivo. Así los fallos esperados (falta de existencias, pago rechazado) son datos que se tratan, no excepciones que se escapan.

`Order.fromJson` usa una lista de inicialización y, dentro, un `for` con un **patrón de lista**: cada línea del JSON es un array `[sku, qty, cents]` que se desestructura y se guarda como un record `(String, int, int)`. `total` suma cantidad por precio con `fold`, y `toJson` devuelve el resumen que se enviará después.

`process` es el servicio asíncrono simulado: espera 10 ms por línea, busca las líneas cuyo producto no tiene existencias suficientes en el mapa `stock` y devuelve un `Err` si encuentra alguna o si el total pasa de 100 euros (10000 céntimos); si no, un `Ok`. Como es `async`, su tipo es `Future<Result<Order>>`.

`main` decodifica los pedidos y los procesa **todos en paralelo** con `Future.wait(orders.map(process))`. Aunque cada uno tarde distinto, los resultados llegan en el orden de los pedidos, así que la salida no cambia. El `switch` sobre el `Result` sellado es exhaustivo y extrae `value` o `reason`; después, `if (r case Ok(:final value))` se queda con los aceptados y `jsonEncode` produce el informe, llamando a `toJson()` de cada pedido.

Clases, records, patrones, genéricos, `async` y JSON, todo en 34 líneas. En DMarlon Studio, Dart es el lenguaje de los destinos Flutter, y este es justo el tipo de código que va en la capa de modelo y lógica de esas aplicaciones, separado de los widgets que lo muestran.
points: Un `Result` sellado convierte los fallos esperados en datos.
Los patrones de lista leen JSON compacto con seguridad.
`Future.wait` procesa en paralelo y mantiene el orden.
El `switch` exhaustivo obliga a tratar el éxito y el error.
`toJson` y `jsonEncode` preparan la salida para otra API.
es.exercise: Añada al informe final un campo `rejected` con la lista de motivos de los pedidos rechazados, obtenida con otro `if (r case Err(:final reason))`.

en.title: Project: order processing
en.summary: Combine Dart sealed classes, generics, async and JSON in a small order processing system: the logic that sits behind a Flutter app.
body: This program brings the course together in a small order processing layer, the kind a Flutter app keeps underneath its screens. It starts with a sealed, generic **`Result<T>`** type: an operation ends either in `Ok`, holding a value, or in `Err`, holding a reason. That way expected failures (out of stock, payment declined) are data you handle, not exceptions that escape.

`Order.fromJson` uses an initializer list and, inside it, a `for` with a **list pattern**: each JSON line is an array `[sku, qty, cents]` that is destructured and stored as a `(String, int, int)` record. `total` adds up quantity times price with `fold`, and `toJson` returns the summary to be sent on later.

`process` is the simulated asynchronous service: it waits 10 ms per line, looks for lines whose product lacks enough units in the `stock` map, and returns an `Err` if it finds one or if the total exceeds 100 euros (10000 cents); otherwise, an `Ok`. Being `async`, its type is `Future<Result<Order>>`.

`main` decodes the orders and processes **all of them in parallel** with `Future.wait(orders.map(process))`. Even though each takes a different time, the results arrive in order, so the output never changes. The `switch` over the sealed `Result` is exhaustive and extracts `value` or `reason`; then `if (r case Ok(:final value))` keeps the accepted ones and `jsonEncode` produces the report, calling each order's `toJson()`.

Classes, records, patterns, generics, `async` and JSON, all in 34 lines. In DMarlon Studio, Dart is the language of the Flutter targets, and this is exactly the kind of code that goes into the model and logic layer of those apps, kept apart from the widgets that display it.
points: A sealed `Result` turns expected failures into data.
List patterns read compact JSON safely.
`Future.wait` processes in parallel and keeps the order.
The exhaustive `switch` forces you to handle both success and failure.
`toJson` and `jsonEncode` prepare the output for another API.
en.exercise: Add a `rejected` field to the final report with the list of reasons for the rejected orders, gathered with another `if (r case Err(:final reason))`.

advanced.html: import 'dart:convert';// Either a value or the reason it failed: a switch must handle both.sealed class Result<T> {}class Ok<T> extends Result<T> { final T value; Ok(this.value); }class Err<T> extends Result<T> { final String reason; Err(this.reason); }class Order {  final String id;  final List<(String sku, int qty, int cents)> lines;  Order.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> json) : id = json['id'],        lines = [for (final [String sku, int qty, int cents] in json['lines']) (sku, qty, cents)];  int get total => lines.fold(0, (sum, line) => sum + line.$2 * line.$3);  Map<String, dynamic> toJson() => {'id': id, 'total': total};}const stock = {'MUG': 5, 'TEE': 0, 'CAP': 3};Future<Result<Order>> process(Order order) async { // a simulated service  await Future.delayed(Duration(milliseconds: 10 * order.lines.length));  final missing = order.lines.where((line) => (stock[line.$1] ?? 0) < line.$2);  if (missing.isNotEmpty) return Err('${order.id}: no stock of ${missing.first.$1}');  return order.total > 10000 ? Err('${order.id}: payment declined') : Ok(order);}const incoming = '[{"id": "A-1", "lines": [["MUG", 2, 1250]]}, {"id": "A-2", "lines": [["CAP", 1, 1500], '    '["TEE", 1, 1999]]}, {"id": "A-3", "lines": [["CAP", 3, 4000]]}, {"id": "A-4", "lines": [["MUG", 1, 1250]]}]';Future<void> main() async {  final orders = [for (final json in jsonDecode(incoming)) Order.fromJson(json)];  final results = await Future.wait(orders.map(process)); // all in parallel  for (final result in results) print(switch (result) {        Ok(:final value) => 'OK    ${value.id}: ${value.total} cents',        Err(:final reason) => 'ERROR $reason',      });  final accepted = [for (final r in results) if (r case Ok(:final value)) value];  print(jsonEncode({'accepted': accepted, 'revenue': accepted.fold(0, (s, o) => s + o.total)}));}

OK    A-1: 2500 cents
ERROR A-2: no stock of TEE
ERROR A-3: payment declined
OK    A-4: 1250 cents
{"accepted":[{"id":"A-1","total":2500},{"id":"A-4","total":1250}],"revenue":3750}
